I at the outset sincerely congratulate the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) for having moved this resolution, which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the amending of the Old Age Pension Act at an early date so as to extend its provisions to the Indians of Canada.
I endorse this resolution wholeheartedly. There is in my constituency a very important group of Hurons, and I may state that they are as intelligent as any member of the House of Commons. They have set up industries which support a part of the population; several of them hold important positions either in business or in industry, and still others have gained recognition in the field of arts, science and letters. Furthermore, I wish to point out to the house that several of those Indians have been on active service overseas and some who belong to the best families of the Huron reserve of Loretteville, have been decorated by His Majesty the King.
Now, Mr. Speaker, you may wonder how it is that a Huron settlement is located so near Quebec city. A while ago, the hon. member for Lake St. John-Roberval (Mr. Dion) explained the various migrations of another tribe of Indians, the Montagnais, since the very beginning of the colony. In his general dictionary on Canada, Reverend Father Lejeune, O.M.I., has this to say about Loretteville:
At the time of Cartier (1535-42), the two settlements of Stadacona and Hochelaga were peopled by the Huron-Iroquois nations: the study of 160 Indian words, collected by the discoverer, supports this assertion. By 1603, when Champlain made his first trip and sailed up the St. Lawrence as far as the Sault, a fierce enmity divided the Hurons and Iroquois; only the Algonquins, allies of the Hurons, still peopled the shores of the river. Champlain embraced their cause.
The expedition he was almost compelled to lead against the Tsonnontouans in 1615, fired the Five Nations with a fierce and unrelenting hatred for the French and their allies. They vented their rage ceaselessly, and once they had found in fire-arms an outlet for their hatred, they used them with audacity and violence after trading with the white man. The Huron population was constantly on the wane because of the ravages of endemic outbreaks ot disease. Further, Champlain, in spite of his foresight and pressing entreaties -was taken in and disarmed by the successive companies: what manpower reinforcements could he guarantee his
allies? His last appeal to Richelieu himself (made- in August 1635) remained unanswered. Once armed, it was clear sailing for the furious Iroquois. In June 1642, they struck a first blow at the settlement of Contarea, "main artery of the Huron country", located 5 miles southeast of Orillia. We know what followed: from 1647 to 1650, the Huron, Petune and Neutral Nations were pillaged, sacked, annihilated almost, except for the small groups that fled afar. Missionaries were tortured, burned at the stake and devoured. (See Brebeuf, Lalemant, Daniel, Gamier.) .	.	. Had the
assembled tribes thought of organizing mass united resistance, the Iroquois would never have bested their combined action. The hour of exile tolled for all surviving groups.
The Recollets were the first to sojourn among the Hurons and their neighbouring tribes; three priests and one brother visited them but, as they lacked all knowledge of the Indian idiom, their efforts were fruitless. From 1615 to 1629, two Jesuits became their collaborators; from 1634 to 1650, these two were the only missionaries for that district. Their main residence was at Ste. Marie du Sault, and from there, they visited the various missions surrounding them. More than 25 priests and an important group of coadjutors, benevolent workers and paid help worked for the conversion and salvation of the Hurons and their allies. The converts were numerous, but the tribes were to be massacred and disbanded for a long time.
At the present, there are three groups who survived the slaughter: the Hurons of Jeune-Lorette, three leagues from Quebec; those of the Sandwich district, in the county of Essex (Ontario); and the Hurons of the Wyandot reservation, in the state of Oklahoma (United States). The first group, numbering about 300, in 1650, took refuge at Sillery, under the guns of fort St. Louis, in the city of Quebec. The following year, they went to the isle of Orleans, on a plot of land ceded to them by Eleonore de Grandmaison, widow of Francois de Chavigny; in 1654, a group of their former tribe, who had taken refuge, first iij Manitoulin island and then in Three Rivers, joined them, raising their numbers to about 600. On May-20, 1656, 40 canoes bearing Agniers Indians launch a suprise attack on their island, capturing or killing 71 of them: this bold attack caused the Huron colony to return to the protection of Quebec city. The following year, from June to August, numerous detachments decide to request shelter from their enemies, while the remainder stay at the Fort des Hurons. In 1660, 40 of the most intrepid among them go to Montreal and join the small expedition of the gallant Dollard des Ormeaux. In April, 1668, the Fort colony transfers to the C6te de Beauport, a league removed from the capital city. The following year, it migrates to^Cbte St. Michel or Notre Dame de Foy. In 1673, new migration to Vieille Lorette; and, finally, in 1697, to Jeune Lorette, their present abode.
These Indians, whose number has greatly been reduced in the last seven years, form in my constituency, a group of people who render great services to the whole community. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since 1763, when Canada was ceded to Great Britain, the Indians in this country have been regarded as independent Indian nations under the protection of the crown. In the county of Bonaventure, which I represent iu this chamber, we have two Indian reserves, one in Maria East, and one at Ste. Anne de Restigouche. The total Indian population on these two reserves at the last federal census in 1941 was 871 souls. These Indians are Micmacs, a branch of the Algonkian tribe, whose total population in the eastern part of Canada at the present time is about 4,000 souls. In Bonaventure county, if we refer to the last federal census, we find that the population of Micmac Indians has increased by over forty per cent since 1911. That is a good sign, a healthy sign. It means that the population of Bonaventure county is very kind to them. These Micmac Indians are very industrious, clever, respectful of the law and peaceful. They are first-class fishing guides; they certainly know how to handle a canoe and drown a salmon. They do a lot of fishing in the summer time and hunting throughout the winter. They also

Old Age Pensions-Indians
make fine baskets, which they sell to tourists; they do very little farming. They have their schools and their church. They are good citizens and good Christians. Most of them are almost of pure blood, and they retain most of their primitive characteristics.
At the time of the coming of the white man, it will probably interest the house to know, these tribes of Algonkians and Micmacs occupied all the eastern part of Canada, including Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, the coastal region of New Brunswick, and the Gaspe coast, comprising the present counties of Gaspe, Bonaventure and Matapedia. The name "Micmac" is an Algonkian word which means "allies". As a matter of fact we owe these Micmac Indians many names of places along the Gaspe peninsula and throughout the eastern part of our country. May I recall here to the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Langlois) that the word "Gaspe" is a Micmac word which means "the end", "the extremity". But had it not been for the Micmac Indians, when Jacques Cartier landed at Gaspe there would have been nobody there to meet him. They greeted Cartier in 1534 at Gaspe when the French explorer took possession of this country in the name of Christ and the king of France and laid the foundation of a new colony which was to become the cradle of Canadian civilization.
An interesting Castilian legend tells that early explorers in searching for gold wandered along the coast of Gaspe and Bonaventure county in the baie des Chaleurs as far as the mouth of the Restigouche river, where there is an Indian reserve of Micmacs to-day, and, finding no gold, simply wrote on a rock "Aca nada", which meant "there is nothing here."

The early French settlers in Acadia succeeded in winning the friendship of those Algonkian and Micmac Indians to the extent that when Acadia was ceded to Great Britain in 1713, English settlement in the country was impossible on any extensive scale for half a century, and at the time of the dispersion of the Acadians in 1755, thanks to the cooperation of those Indians-who were very likely the paratroopers of those days-many Acadians escaped through the woods of New Brunswick and reached what is to-day called Bonaventure county, where my own ancestors 47696-93
established themselves in 1758. I never could find out exactly what amount of gratitude my ancestors owed to those Indians, but I would not be surprised if those Micmacs and Algonkians helped them to flee from the bad men-I was just going to say, from the Tories -of that time. Therefore I am in favour of the resolution of the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness).

speechtext:
The hon. member will find that on private members day we have leeway to discuss a question from all the angles and we deal with old age pension for the Indians. I repeat that I have no intention of being an obstructionist or of detaining the house, but it has been almost impossible for me hitherto to put forward the problems pertaining to my own section of northern Ontario for nearly three years.
I have there what we call Moose Factory and Moosonee. These are historic names, connected as they are with the history of such

Old Age Pensions-Indians

firms as Hudson's Bay company and Revillon Freres. In my constituency are areas where hundreds, indeed thousands of Indians are living at the present time. To say that I am absolutely satisfied with all that has been done for the Indians would not be truthful, but Canada has done better for its Indian population than some other countries have done for theirs, because some other countries ^ have stated in the past that a good Indian is the one who is six feet under ground. To our honour and good name we have never acted on that principle in this country. You have only to read the history of French-speaking and English-speaking Canada to realize how much we have tried, through our missionaries as well as through our own European or American civilization, to improve the lot of the Indian, although we still have a long way to go yet on that score.
I am glad that the hon. member for Calgary East saw fit to introduce this resolution and I am satisfied that he is fully protected by the statement made by the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen), who spoke so force-, fully and sympathetically of the problems relating to our Indians. He said that he was not one hundred per cent satisfied with all that had been done, and he intends that more will be accomplished. Speaking of my own section of the country, I have had some experience among the Indians themselves. It has never been found possible to properly try agriculture among the Indians; that is what we have been told. Whether that is due to climatic conditions or to other circumstances, the fact is that we have never -really tried to make farmers out of Indians. In my opinion that was a glaring error. Take some of the lands around Lowbush, Cochrane, Mattice- I do not mention Moose Factory or Moosonee. These lands are eminently suited to agriculture, and in this connection I would quote the words of a late lamented bishop of the Anglican church, Bishop Anderson, whose see was in the town of Cochrane and in whose veins, I believe, there flowed some Indian blood. He was wrapped up in his work among the Indians; and what marvellous work he did among them. He called them his Indians, and he told me on several occasions that, while it might have been all right at one time to leave the Indians to their happy hunting grounds, times had changed, and that in his opinion, it should be found feasible now, not only in Ontario but throughout Canada, to make real farmers and craftsmen of our Indians. He struck me as being sincerely convinced of this possibility.
In our section of the country, it would seem, the moment we settled northern

Ontario after the construction of the Canadian National railway line from Quebec to Winnipeg, the coming of the white people among the Indians proved, not a blessing, but to some extent a curse to those people. I say that deliberately and with some knowledge of what happened.
This is neither the time nor the place to criticize the actions of people in the past, but speaking of the hunting ground of the Indians, I maintain that any provincial government-and this should apply just as well to the northwest territories-should preserve a strict line of demarcation between the domain of the Indians and the territory operated by white trappers. That line of demarcation should be well defined; otherwise, the mo'ment the - white trappers come in, where Indians have been hunting for generations and for centuries, their tendency is to destroy the natural habitat of the Indian.
In my section of the countiy the experience has been that the moment white trappers came among the Indians there was a conflict, where there was no disharmony beforej while the Indians were left alone. I must commend the' Ontario government, through its protective department of lands and forests, for having in the last six years created a great reserve north of the Canadian National, between that line and James -bay basin, taking in some 25,000 square miles* where at present fur-bearing animals such as beaver, otter and mink are being raised and cultivated. If there is one wish I would express this afternoon it is that the provincial government would see to it that ninety per cent, or at least eighty per cent of that territory is kept as a reserve for Indian trappers.
I have seen many sad things happen in Moose Factory and Moosonee section and west of the town of Hearst on the Canadian National transcontinental line, from Hearst to Winnipeg. With the advent of white trappers to the trapping grounds of the Indians discord appeared. There was friction and fighting and sometimes bloodshed. Although some of these things have not been put on the official record, I speak feelingly of them now and I know the minister will do his best to improve matters.
As has been well said this afternoon, the Indians are, after all, the first citizens of Canada. The -record of our dealings with [DOT]them in the past has not always been admirable, but at any rate it will bear comparison with any other nation's treatment of similar inhabitants. This House of Commons has jurisdiction over our Indians, and it is the duty of parliament to do everything possible for that population. I have not the statis-

Business oj the House
tics before me at the .moment, but I believe that the Indians in war number one, my section, as well as those in war number two, enlisted in such numbers that the ratio to their population is as large as that in any other section of the country. May I say this to hon. members. If I thought for one moment that the passing of this resolution, which I have no doubt will cariy unanimously, would help to improve the lot of the Indians I would sit down at once, but at the same time I submit that I have a right to put forward my views before this national forum and to say what has happened in my own section of the country. If I thought that the Minister of Mines and Resources had not in mind the immediate implementing of all that he said this afternoon I would not speak now. But I do not think anyone will seriously doubt the sincerity of a man who speaks as earnestly as I am speaking now, for the good reason [DOT]that I know what happened in some sections of my own constituency, and who want to see their lot improved.
I know of incidents that have been deplorable. Indians have occupied a certain piece of land for a number of years, and they have a right to be protected no matter how filthy some people might think them or how badly kept that land may be. I remember what happened in Mattice. There was a proposal to move the Indian tribe from that district along the Canadian National line and bring them to the southern part of the country on the Canadian Pacific railway, but these people came to me and implored me to plead with the "great white chief" to let them remain where their ancestors had been buried along the river that passes through Mattice. The government is fully aware of these facts.
I have had access to the Indian department in Ottawa time and again; I have seen the officials in my own section of the country, and from my experience I would say that if you put your case before the proper authorities with sincerity and knowledge you are sure to have a solution in the near future.
I have no time now to discuss other questions, but before I conclude I hope it will be found possible in the estimates of the department to build a hospital, not on the shores of James bay but at Cochrane on the Ontario side, where the Indians in northern Ontario among whom I have lived so many years, will find it possible to secure proper accommodation, which they have not at the moment. I sincerely express that hope and I know that 47696-93i
the minister will do all that he can to make it a realization. Nothing short of that will satisfy the country.
Before taking my seat I wish to thank hon. members for allowing me to speak on this subject. The situation is not a pleasant one on account of the lateness of the hour. I see some hon. members smiling, but I do not think anyone will doubt me when I say that I have worked and suffered for these people. I have gone to the police magistrate to fight their case, charging them nothing, but exerting myself doing all that I possibly could on, their behalf to find a solution for their problems. That is why I have made this statement to our national forum, and I will again take the opportunity to speak for our Indians when the proper estimates are before the committee.

speechtext: The first order of business to-morrow will be the'bill of the Minister of Reconstruction, which I believe is No. 25 on the order paper. The minister spoke to me last night about this matter. I realize the government has the responsibility of determining the programme to be followed by parliament; the rest of us, being in the minority, necessarily accept that programme. The minister has satisfied me that the measure he is bringing forward to-morrow is pressing, but I just want to say that there is a major measure which has been before parliament for a month, the most important business proposal before parliament, and not a single item of any of those estimates has been passed. I have discussed the matter on several occasions with
Business of the House

the acting leader of the government and he has undertaken to see that this measure would be given right of way. Since then, however, other measures have been brought forward. We had the food and agriculture organization resolution, the united nations resolution, the measure moved by the Minister of Reconstruction the other day, and now this.
I do wish to protest against the treatment this important measure is receiving from parliament. We have a proposed expenditure of $5,000 million; seven months of the year have passed, and that proportion of the estimates have been voted; probably most of the money has been spent, and I expect that soon the government will be coming forward again to ask for another interim supply bill. I think they should realize the position in which this puts members of the house, because no doubt shortly there will be a rush to terminate the business of this session of parliament, and these important measures will be put through without adequate consideration. ' The government do not require our .approval of their plans to carry on, and I assured the Minister of Finance yesterday that we would not stand in the way of his proposals; but I also explained to him that we would have to protest that this other measure is not receiving the consideration it should be given bjr this parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should like to modify what I said to this extent, that I may take up the housing resolution first to-morrow rather than have the measure of the Minister of Reconstruction taken up first. I should like to leave the government that option. Then, after moving that resolution, I would be prepared to go right back to the war appropriation. I understand the importance of getting ahead with those estimates. In other years we have discussed the war appropriation measure for four, five or six weeks, and as a result a large mass of legislation was brought forward towards the end of the session, bringing upon us severe criticism for having followed that course. The government cannot do everything. It is not derelict; it is ready with its business, but we just have to take the most important business first. I would not be putting forward this housing resolution to-morrow unless it were urgent; but if it meets the wishes of the house once I have moved that resolution we can move the adjournment of the debate and go right on with the war appropriation. Of course this suggestion may not be acceptable to hon. members, either; they may wish to debate the housing resolution.
I think if the minister makes a statement to-morrow in support of his legislation, hon. members should be given the right to say something in reply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

Could not the whips of the parties get together and try to eliminate the constant repetition of questions? During the past few days we have had so much repetition of the same questions and the same statements that we may not get through the business of the house at all. It seems to me an attempt should be made to see that a certain line of questioning is pursued by a certain member to a conclusive point, and then have done with it; get all the information we can and then have someone start on some other questions. As a matter of fact that is the way we are trying to organize our work. If we could all do that, I think we would accelerate and facilitate the business of this house. There is so much repetition that it makes it bad for all of us. I am referring to plans for the further discussion of the war estimates, of course.
